MERIDA return to the WorldTour – Does the switch make sense for Soudal–Safety Jogger?

4 days ago
by Benedikt Ueberholz
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 9:50
Instaread


Tom Boonen won the biggest Classics on a Specialized. Remco Evenepoel rode one to the team’s first Grand Tour victory. From 2027, Tim Merlier and Paul Magnier will be sprinting for wins on MERIDA bikes. Soudal–Safety Jogger are trading the winner of our all-round race bike group test for the winner of our aero bike group test. Sounds like a pretty good deal for the two sprinters. But what’s in it for the climbers?

In 18 seasons on bikes bearing the big S, the team racked up 800 wins, took dozens of Monuments and broke the record for Tour stage wins. With Marcel Kittel on the Venge ViAS, they even helped bring disc brakes into the peloton. Standard kit today, they were hugely controversial at the time, with plenty of riders convinced they could cost someone their life. Now the Belgian outfit have a new name and a new bike sponsor. From 2027, Soudal–Safety Jogger will ride MERIDA bikes on an initial four-year deal, as will the AG Insurance–Soudal women’s team. It’s the REACTO for road stages and the TIME WARP for time trials. For the team, it’s the end of an era twice over. Specialized are leaving after nearly 20 years, and for the first time since the team was founded in 2003, Quick-Step are leaving too.

We’ll get used to the new bikes soon enough. As for getting the team name right every time, consider this our apology in advance.

Why MERIDA, and why now?

If the name REACTO still brings to mind Sonny Colbrelli lying in the Roubaix velodrome in 2021, caked in mud and crying tears of joy, you already have part of the answer. Pro racing has shaped MERIDA’s identity ever since they joined forces with Lampre in 2013. Their closest ties were with Bahrain, first as title sponsors alongside Vincenzo Nibali from 2017, then as bike suppliers until the end of 2025. Few riders gave those bikes better stories than Matej Mohorič. In 2022, he hit the dropper lever on his SCULTURA on the descent of the Poggio and rode to victory in Milan–San Remo. A year later, he rode the SILEX to its first gravel world title. After a season without a WorldTour team, MERIDA are back on the stage where those memories are made.

The move seems to make sense for Specialized too. MERIDA own a 35% stake in Specialized, which is why, for instance, they don’t sell bikes in the US. Seen in that light, the switch looks more like a way of spreading their sponsorship around than losing a team to a rival.

In the men’s WorldTour, Specialized still have Red Bull–BORA–hansgrohe and Remco, who also has a personal deal with the brand. Red Bull’s international reach extends well into the all-important US market. MERIDA, meanwhile, get a direct line to European fans through a Belgian Classics team. The two brands’ interests are more closely aligned than the logos suggest, and this split should let each reach its audience without treading on the other’s toes. As for how much the deal with Quick-Step – sorry, Soudal–Safety Jogger – is worth, the figures doing the rounds are € 6–8 million for MERIDA against € 4 million for Specialized. If those numbers are right, MERIDA are digging considerably deeper than the Californians, though the length of the previous partnership may have something to do with that. In interviews, the team insist they tested several brands on the road and in the wind tunnel, and that the results counted for more than the money.

From Tarmac to REACTO. Who comes out ahead?

We can see the racing logic. The MERIDA REACTO TEAM won our aero road bike group test. The catch? The Wolfpack are giving up the S-Works Tarmac SL9, the standout bike in our latest all-round race bike group test. You can read it in the new issue. With sprinters Magnier and Merlier the team’s two stars, putting them on the best aero bike looks like an upgrade.

All change, except the groupset

The Tarmac is only the start of what’s disappearing from the team bus. Until now, Specialized supplied the wheels, tyres, saddles, helmets and shoes too.

Wheels: from Roval to Shimano

Shimano stay on for groupsets and pedals and will now supply the wheels too. The Roval Rapide CLX III and Roval Sprint make way for DURA-ACE wheels with 36, 50 and 60 mm rim depths. We’ve ridden both the Rapide CLX III and the DURA-ACE C50 (also in the latest issue). Both are accomplished all-rounders with carbon spokes, and we’d struggle to pick between them. With the previous generation of Shimano wheels, we’d have gone straight for the Rovals.

Tyres: from Specialized to Conti

The tyre swap brings a gain you can measure. The S-Works Turbo TLR and RapidAir TLR make way for Continental’s GP 5000 S TR and GP 5000 TT TR. That gives the Wolfpack the most versatile race tyre in our group test and, for the fast days, the one with the lowest rolling resistance. In our road tyre group test, Conti’s quickest setup beat the fastest Specialized pairing by just over two watts. Whether the aero-optimised Aero 111 will find its way onto the front wheel is still an open question. It’s a rare sight on other teams’ bikes.

Helmets: from Specialized to Lazer

Lazer take over helmet duties from the airy Prevail and the S-Works Evade 4. We’d expect to see the Vento aero helmet on most stages. We’ve yet to test it, but it has a tough act to follow. The Evade is one of our favourites and few aero helmets are quite so versatile.

Saddles: from Specialized to Prologo

Prologo take over at the saddle. The 3D-printed S-Works Power was one of the few saddles everyone on our editorial team could get on with. Prologo bring a wide range of race saddles to choose from, right up to the aero-optimised Choice. An aero saddle on an aero bike? On looks alone, we’re sold.

Shoes: from Specialized to SIDI

The riders may feel the switch most keenly at their feet. Plenty get on well with Specialized’s Body Geometry design, with its distinctive varus wedge that tilts the foot slightly. After thousands of kilometres riding like that, you might well notice a change of shoes more than a couple of watts at the tyres. Until now, the team also used Specialized’s in-house Retül system for bike fits and custom footbeds. For some riders, those footbeds increased the tilt further. Who’ll handle bike fitting and footbeds from here is still unclear.

SIDI are known for a narrow fit, but they also make bespoke shoes for the pros and keep the riders’ lasts in their workshop like trophies. We’re particularly keen to see more of the lace-up race shoes SIDI showed at Rouleur Live in November. Isaac del Toro had already ridden them to a Tour podium. Some teams let riders choose their own shoes, so we’re curious to see how SIDI find a fit for the entire squad. If they don’t, it might take less than a savage attack to put a grimace on a rider’s face.

Handlebars: from Roval to MERIDA, or will it be Vision?

At the bars, it comes down to millimetres. We loved the way the Tarmac’s Roval Rapide cockpit felt in our hands. MERIDA’s own cockpit made headlines at the REACTO launch mainly for how narrow it was. At the time, MERIDA judged it too narrow for UCI racing, so they also offered the bike with a Vision Metron 5D cockpit. Yet two of the three MERIDA sizes measure more than 400 mm across the drops and should, on that basis, be legal. And which cockpit is in the team photos released so far? The very MERIDA bar whose legality is in question. Whether it can be raced, and in what configuration, remains to be seen. There’s a similar question hanging over the brake cooling fins, which MERIDA say improve both cooling and aerodynamics. On the previous REACTO, the UCI classed them as aerodynamic fairings, which are banned in competition. Yet there they are in the first team photos.

What will the Wolfpack ride in the mountains?

The REACTO is light for a dedicated aero bike, but getting a race-ready build down to the UCI’s 6.8 kg limit could be tricky. Without a UDH mount, we wouldn’t expect to see the team chasing grams with a 1x build just yet. That leaves the SCULTURA. Its comfort won us over on our first ride, but that was back in 2021. It’s now one of the oldest race bikes in the peloton, and bikes like the Tarmac have pulled ahead on both weight and aerodynamics.

A new SCULTURA that paired the comfort of the old bike with up-to-date aerodynamics and a bit less weight would be welcome news for the climbers. Perhaps that’s another attraction of the deal for MERIDA. As George Hincapie often points out, a pro team developing a race bike can give you feedback no wind tunnel can. There’s been no word of a successor yet. For Merlier and Magnier, the REACTO already adds up.

If you were running the team and had your pick of bike sponsors for 2027, would you go with MERIDA or Specialized? And would you give the same answer on the flat roads of the spring Classics as you would deep into an epic Tour mountain stage?

About the Author

Benedikt Ueberholz
Junior Editor

Benedikt Ueberholz is a junior editor at 41 Publishing, specialising in road cycling and performance. With a master’s degree in Sports Management, his academic research into bike retail and cycling sponsorship provide the theoretical foundation for his work. Covering around 45,000 kilometres a year on his road bike, with international racing experience under his belt, he brings extensive hands-on expertise to individual and group reviews. His focus? Aerodynamics, components, bike set-up and in-depth evaluations of high-performance road bikes.
